name: Nara
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Abushush Dawd & Richard J. Hayward. 2002. Nara. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 32(2): 249-255. DOI 10.1017/S0025100302001068 (Illustrations of the IPA; open access on Cambridge Core).
catalog_locator: Section 'Tone', pp. 249-250: opening sentences p. 249; stress statement in the last paragraph of the section, p. 250.
catalog_quote: Nara is a tone language. The tone-bearing unit is the mora and, in addition to vowels, post-vocalic glides and sonorant consonants also carry tone. Tones are associated independently with each mora of a long vowel. Monomoraic (short open) syllables carry either higher or lower relatively level pitch, and these are interpreted as high (H) and low (L) tones, respectively ... Bimoraic (CVV and CVC) syllables have an additional two pitch patterns, viz. falling and rising contours ... These contours are straightforwardly interpretable as sequences of the H and L tones. ... Rather, we suggest, this tonal perturbation is motivated by a phonological constraint that disallows two non-contiguous High tones within a phonological phrase. Thompson (1976: 484) makes certain tentative comments about stress in Nara, but we find no convincing evidence for this additional prosodic feature, and the examples adduced by Thompson seem to lend themselves to a simpler analysis in terms of length (gemination) of the following consonant.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (7 pp., JIPA 32/2, DOI 10.1017/S0025100302001068, Cambridge Core download footer) opened with extracted text. The quote is there verbatim: the 'Tone' section opens on p. 249 with 'Nara is a tone language. The tone-bearing unit is the mora and, in addition to vowels, post-vocalic glides and sonorant consonants also carry tone. Tones are associated independently with each mora of a long vowel.' and the last paragraph of the section on p. 250 reads 'Thompson (1976: 484) makes certain tentative comments about stress in Nara, but we find no convincing evidence for this additional prosodic feature, and the examples adduced by Thompson seem to lend themselves to a simpler analysis in terms of…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nara is a two-tone (H/L) mora-tone language; the JIPA authors explicitly find no evidence for word stress as a separate prosodic feature and reanalyse Thompson's (1976: 484) 'stress on any syllable, contrastive' examples ('iŋŋa vs iŋ'ŋa) as gemination of the following consonant. The one older source with an accent rule, Reinisch 1874 (pp. 19-20, from Munzinger's acute marks), restricts the 'accent' to one of the last three syllables of the word, never retracting beyond the antepenult, staying on the stem syllable under plural suffixation (suffix never accented), with penult accent in -ado/-edo abstract nouns and person-dependent accent in verb paradigms (p. 61) - a lexical/morphological accent within a three-syllable window that most plausibly records the high tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Thompson 1976 p. 484 claims contrastive stress on any syllable, with 'CVCV -> 'CVCCV gemination after a stressed first syllable; Abushush & Hayward 2002 reject this as stress. Reinisch 1874 notes his manuscript inconsistently gives dlédo 'gang' beside the penult rule for -ado/-edo nouns.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (moras; citation forms), with a phonological-phrase constraint against two non-contiguous H tones that deletes an expected H on the syntactic head; the stress denial concerns the word. Speaker described: Higir dialect (higi1240).
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source (Abushush & Hayward 2002) describes the speech of one 31-year-old male speaker of the Higir dialect (higi1240, Eastern Nara), the basis of the emerging standard; Hayward 2000 is likewise Higir. Thompson 1976 'Nera' and Reinisch 1874 'Barea' (Munzinger's 1860s manuscript material) are the same language under older names, dialect unspecified.

tone_statements.citation: Savà, Graziano. 2024. An account of recent research on Nara: tone, plural and texts. Ethnorema 20: 61-68. DOI 10.23814/ethn.20.24.sav
tone_statements.quote: About tone it is simply stated that there is a “normal” and a “high” tone (Thompson 1976: 484). What is called stress is rather tone in later descriptions by other authors. ... Hayward (2000, 23 pages) and Abushush and Hayward (2002, six pages) have roughly the same content. After discussing the inventory of Nara consonants and vowels, the papers go into details into the tone system of Higir. It is restated that there are two tones H and L but that some of the words have falling tones on short vowels, such as bûk “dove”. It is also determined that no HLH sequence is allowed in the language and that a sandhi phenomena adjusts the situation when needed. ... I took particular note of tonal minimal pairs such as ...: làá spear làà necklace túsá urine tùsà ears
tone_statements.locator: p. 62, section 2 'Previous research on Nara'; minimal pairs p. 64, section 3
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones H and L (secondhand from Hayward 2000 / Abushush & Hayward 2002, endorsed), falling tone possible on some short vowels (bûk 'dove'), rising/falling on long vowels written as tone sequences (làá vs làà); no HLH sequence permitted, repaired by tone sandhi; lexical tone minimal pairs on nouns and grammatical tone (singular/plural pairs such as bállá 'legs' vs bállà 'leg', káttà 'ax'…

sources.note: pp. 249-250 'Tone': Nara is a tone language (H/L on moras; contours = tone sequences; H dropped on phrase heads to avoid two non-contiguous Hs in a phonological phrase); p. 250: Thompson (1976: 484) makes tentative comments about stress, 'but we find no convincing evidence for this additional prosodic feature' - his examples are reanalysed as gemination of the following consonant. Speaker: Higir dialect.

sources.citation: Reinisch, Leo. 1874. Die Barea-Sprache: Grammatik, Text und Wörterbuch (nach den handschriftlichen Materialien von Werner Munzinger Pascha). Wien: Wilhelm Braumüller. (Google scan, archive.org item diebareasprache00reingoog)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number 2246.97)
sources.note: Lautlehre pp. 19-20 (pp. 56-57; page scan saved): accent = Munzinger's acute; 'Der accent kann nur auf einer der drei lezten silben des wortes ruhen'; never retracts beyond the antepenult (adjective plurals antepenult); otherwise stays on the stem syllable in the plural (hágga pl. hággita); plural suffix never accented; abstract nouns in -ado/-edo accented on the penult. p. 61 (p. 110): passive perfect accent on the penult in 1pl, antepenult in the other persons. No tone recognised.

sources.citation: Thompson, David E. 1976. Nera. In M. Lionel Bender (ed.), The Non-Semitic Languages of Ethiopia, 484-494. East Lansing: African Studies Center, Michigan State University. (Only p. 484 opened: Rosetta Project excerpt on archive.org, item rosettaproject_nrb_phon-1)
sources.note: p. 484 §2.2 Stress: 'Stress may come on any syllable and can cause change of meaning, e.g. 'iŋŋa "you (singular)", iŋ'ŋa "you (plural)". When the first of two CV syllables is stressed, the second C becomes doubled with short vowels: 'CVCV -> 'CVCCV.' §2.3 Tone: 'At least two significant tones occur: normal and high.' (page scan verified:)
